items.subject: QR
items.subskill: probability on a spinner with unequal sections
items.prompt: The spinner is divided into the three sections shown. If the arrow is spun once, what is the probability that it lands on green?
items.explanation: The green section takes up half of the spinner, the same space as red and blue together. So the arrow lands on green 1 out of 2 times.
items.misconceptions: treats unequal sections as equally likely

why.A: 1 out of 4 is the chance of landing on red (or on blue); green is twice as big as each of them.
why.B: 1 out of 3 treats the three sections as the same size; green covers half of the spinner.
why.D: 3 out of 4 is the chance of NOT landing on red — a different question.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: probability of a factor on a numbered spinner
items.prompt: The spinner has eight equal sections numbered 1 to 8. If the arrow is spun once, what is the probability that it lands on a number that is a factor of 6?
items.explanation: The factors of 6 are 1, 2, 3 and 6, and all four are on the spinner. That is 4 out of 8 equal sections, which is the same chance as 1 out of 2.
items.misconceptions: forgets 1 and the number itself are factors

why.B: 1 out of 4 counts only 2 and 3; 1 and 6 are factors of 6 as well.
why.C: 3 out of 8 forgets that 1 is a factor of every number: 1 × 6 = 6.
why.A: 1 out of 8 counts only the 6 itself; 1, 2 and 3 are factors of 6 too.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: reading one circle of a Venn diagram
items.prompt: Ms. Lee asked the 19 students in her class whether they play soccer or the piano. The Venn diagram shows the results. How many students play soccer?
items.explanation: Everyone inside the soccer circle plays soccer, including the overlap. 7 + 4 = 11. The 19 in the question is the whole class, which this question does not need.
items.misconceptions: reads only the outer part of a circle

why.B: 4 is only the students who do both; the soccer players who do not play piano count too.
why.C: 7 is only the part of the soccer circle outside the piano circle; the 4 in the middle play soccer as well.
why.A: 3 is the students outside both circles, who play neither soccer nor the piano.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: total from a Venn diagram
items.prompt: The Venn diagram shows how many students in a club have a dog, a cat, both or neither. How many students are in the club?
items.explanation: Each student is in exactly one region. 9 + 3 + 6 + 2 = 20.
items.misconceptions: counts the overlap twice; forgets the outside region

why.A: 15 adds only the dog-only and cat-only parts (9 + 6), missing the 3 with both and the 2 with neither.
why.B: 18 leaves out the 2 students outside both circles; they are in the club too.
why.D: 23 counts the 3 students with both pets twice; each student is in only one region.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: regions of a three-circle Venn diagram
items.prompt: The Venn diagram shows which sports students in a club play. How many students play exactly two of the three sports?
items.explanation: The regions inside exactly two circles are soccer-and-swimming (2), soccer-and-tennis (1) and swimming-and-tennis (3). 2 + 1 + 3 = 6. The center (1) is three sports, so it is left out.
items.misconceptions: includes the center in "exactly two"

why.A: 1 is the center, the student who plays all three sports, not exactly two.
why.C: 7 adds the center too; exactly two means inside two circles and outside the third.
why.D: 19 is everyone who plays at least one sport.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: elapsed time from a clock
items.prompt: The clock shows the time the bus left school. The trip to the zoo took 25 minutes. What time did the bus reach the zoo?
items.explanation: The clock shows 10:50. Ten more minutes is 11:00, and 15 more is 11:15.
items.misconceptions: reads the minute hand's number as minutes; reads the nearest hour

why.A: 10:15 adds 25 minutes but does not move to the next hour after 60 minutes.
why.B: 10:35 reads the minute hand's number as the minutes (10:10); the minute hand on the 10 means 50 minutes.
why.D: 11:25 reads the hour as 11 because the hour hand is close to it; the bus left at 10:50, not 11:00.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: adding a layer of cubes
items.prompt: The block is built from small cubes, each with a volume of 1 cubic inch. Maya adds one more layer on top, exactly like the top layer. What will the volume of the block be then?
items.explanation: The block has 2 layers of 3 × 2 = 6 cubes, so 12 now. One more layer adds 6: 12 + 6 = 18 cubic inches.
items.misconceptions: adds a row instead of a layer; doubles the block

why.D: 36 triples the block (12 × 3); only one layer of 3 × 2 = 6 cubes is added.
why.A: 15 adds only one row of 3; a whole layer is 2 rows deep.
why.C: 24 doubles the whole block; one layer is added, not two.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: unfolding a shape along a fold
items.prompt: The figure is half of a paper shape. The dashed side is the fold. When the paper is unfolded, what shape will it be?
items.explanation: Reflect the triangle across the dashed side, like opening a folded paper. The bottom side doubles to 8 and the two slanted sides match, making one larger triangle with two equal sides.
items.misconceptions: reflects across the wrong side

why.A: A kite would come from reflecting across the long slanted side; the fold here is the upright dashed side.
why.B: A rectangle needs four right angles; the mirror image across the dashed side makes a shape with three corners.
why.C: A square needs four equal sides and four corners; the unfolded shape has three corners.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: using an input/output rule
items.prompt: Use the table to answer the question. If the same rule is used, what is the output when the input is 10?
items.explanation: Each output is double the input plus 3: 2 → 7, 4 → 11, 5 → 13, 8 → 19. For 10: 10 × 2 + 3 = 23.
items.misconceptions: continues the output column instead of using the rule

why.A: 13 only adds 3 (10 + 3); the rule also doubles the input first.
why.B: 20 only doubles (10 × 2); every output is 3 more than double the input.
why.C: 21 adds 2 to the last output; the input went up by 2, so the output goes up by 2 × 2 = 4.

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: finding the rule that fits every row
items.prompt: Use the table to answer the question. Which rule gives each output from its input?
items.explanation: Check every row: 1 × 3 + 1 = 4, 3 × 3 + 1 = 10, 6 × 3 + 1 = 19, 7 × 3 + 1 = 22. The other rules only fit the first row.
items.misconceptions: checks only the first row

why.A: Add 3 works for the first row (1 → 4) but gives 6 for 3, not 10.
why.B: Multiply by 4 works for the first row but gives 12 for 3, not 10.
why.C: Doubling and adding 2 works for the first row but gives 8 for 3, not 10. A rule has to work for every row.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: fraction of a total from a bar graph
items.prompt: Forty students voted for their favorite season. The graph shows the results. What fraction of the students chose summer or winter?
items.explanation: Summer 15 plus winter 5 is 20 students. 20 of 40 is 1/2.
items.misconceptions: uses only one of the two bars

why.A: 1/8 is winter alone (5 of 40).
why.B: 1/5 is the fall bar (8 of 40), the wrong season.
why.C: 3/8 is summer alone (15 of 40); the question asks for summer or winter.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: comparing rows of a pictograph
items.prompt: The pictograph shows how many cups of lemonade a stand sold each day. How many more cups were sold on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
items.explanation: Tuesday has 4 1/2 symbols and Wednesday 2, a difference of 2 1/2 symbols. Each is 6 cups: 2 × 6 = 12, and half a symbol is 3. 12 + 3 = 15 cups.
items.misconceptions: forgets the key; mishandles the half symbol

why.D: 27 is all of Tuesday's cups (4 1/2 × 6); the question asks how many more than Wednesday.
why.A: 12 leaves out Tuesday's half symbol (4 − 2 = 2 symbols); half a symbol is 3 cups.
why.C: 18 counts the half symbol as a whole one; it stands for only 3 cups.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: halfway point on a number line
items.prompt: Use the number line to answer the question. Point M is halfway between point P and point R. What number is at point M?
items.explanation: P is at 15 and R is at 45, 30 apart. Half of 30 is 15, so M is 15 past P: 15 + 15 = 30.
items.misconceptions: gives the half-distance instead of the point

why.A: 15 is how far M is from P (half of 30), not where M is on the line.
why.C: 45 is where R is; M is between P and R.
why.D: 60 adds P and R (15 + 45); halfway is that sum divided by 2.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: completing a rectangle on a grid
items.prompt: Points J, K and L are three corners of a rectangle. Where should point M go to make rectangle JKLM?
items.explanation: M must be straight below L (same across number, 7) and straight across from J (same up number, 3). So M is at (7, 3).
items.misconceptions: swaps the coordinates

why.A: (3, 7) has the right numbers in the wrong order: M is 7 across and 3 up.
why.B: (5, 5) is near the middle of the rectangle, not a corner.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: missing width from the perimeter
items.prompt: The rectangle in the figure has a perimeter of 30 centimeters. What is its width?
items.explanation: Half the perimeter is one length plus one width: 30 ÷ 2 = 15. Take away the length: 15 − 9 = 6 cm.
items.misconceptions: forgets there are two widths

why.B: 12 cm takes away both lengths (30 − 9 − 9) but forgets that the 12 is two widths together.
why.C: 15 cm is half the perimeter, one length and one width together; take away the 9.
why.D: 21 cm takes away only one length; the rectangle has two lengths and two widths.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: comparing a fraction to a shaded part
items.prompt: Use the figure to answer the question. Which fraction is greater than the part of the circle that is shaded?
items.explanation: 3 of 8 parts are shaded, which is less than half (4 of 8). So 1/2 is greater. 1/4 is 2/8, 1/3 is less than 3/8, and 3/10 uses smaller pieces.
items.misconceptions: compares only the top numbers

why.A: 1/4 is 2 of 8 parts, less than the 3 of 8 shaded.
why.B: 3/10 has the same 3 on top, but tenths are smaller pieces than eighths, so it is less.
why.C: 1/3 is a little less than 3/8 (one third of 8 parts is under 3 parts).

items.source: Original content authored for Sheila ISEE

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: which statement a line graph supports
items.prompt: The graph shows how many birds came to a feeder each week. Which statement is true?

choices.A: The most birds came in Week 5.
choices.B: The number of birds went up every week.
choices.C: The same number came in Week 2 and Week 3.
choices.D: Twice as many came in Week 4 as in Week 2.

items.explanation: Weeks 2 and 3 are both at 14, so the line is flat there. Check each statement against the points, not the shape at a glance.
items.misconceptions: reads the last point as the highest; compares with the wrong week

why.A: Week 5 is the last point but not the highest: Week 4 (20) is higher than Week 5 (18).
why.B: It stayed the same from Week 2 to Week 3 and went down from Week 4 to Week 5.
why.D: Week 4 (20) is twice Week 1 (10), not Week 2 (14).

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: choosing the needed column of a table
items.prompt: The table shows fruit sold at a farm stand. Rosa buys 2 bags of apples and 1 bag of pears. How much does she spend?
items.explanation: Use the price column only: 2 bags of apples are 2 × $4 = $8, and a bag of pears is $6. $8 + $6 = $14. The pounds column is extra information.
items.misconceptions: uses the wrong column or row

why.D: $20 buys 2 bags of pears as well (2 × 4 + 2 × 6); she buys only 1 bag of pears.
why.A: $10 buys one bag of each (4 + 6); she buys 2 bags of apples.
why.C: $16 reads the oranges row for the second fruit (2 × 5 + 6).

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: missing value for a target mean
items.prompt: The graph shows how many laps Theo swam from Monday to Thursday. How many laps must he swim on Friday so that he swims an average of 8 laps a day over the five days?
items.explanation: An average of 8 over 5 days is 5 × 8 = 40 laps in all. He has 6 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 28. 40 − 28 = 12 laps on Friday.
items.misconceptions: gives the average instead of the missing value

why.A: 7 is his average so far (28 ÷ 4); Friday has to pull the average up to 8.
why.B: 8 is the average he wants; he is behind, so Friday must be more than 8.
why.D: 40 is the total for all five days (5 × 8); take away the 28 he has already swum.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: side of a shape with equal sides
items.prompt: Every side of the figure is the same length. Its perimeter is 42 inches. How long is one side?
items.explanation: The figure has 6 equal sides, so each is 42 ÷ 6 = 7 inches.
items.misconceptions: miscounts the sides; subtracts instead of dividing

why.A: 6 inches divides by 7; the figure has 6 sides.
why.C: 10.5 inches divides by 4 as if it were a square; count the sides — there are 6.
why.D: 36 inches subtracts the number of sides (42 − 6); share the perimeter among the sides by dividing.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: growing pattern in a table
items.prompt: The table shows how many tiles are in each figure of a pattern. If the pattern continues, how many tiles will Figure 6 have?
items.explanation: Each figure adds 3 tiles: 4, 7, 10, 13, then 16 for Figure 5 and 19 for Figure 6.
items.misconceptions: stops one figure early; uses only the first row

why.A: 16 is Figure 5; Figure 6 is one more step of 3.
why.B: 18 multiplies 6 × 3 but forgets that each figure is 1 more than 3 times its number.
why.D: 24 multiplies 6 × 4, using only the first row (1 → 4).

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: probability from a table of counts
items.prompt: The table shows the marbles in a bag. If one marble is picked without looking, which color has a 1 out of 5 chance of being picked?
items.explanation: There are 6 + 4 + 2 + 8 = 20 marbles. 1 out of 5 is the same as 4 out of 20, and there are 4 blue marbles.
items.misconceptions: forgets to find the total first

why.B: Green is 2 of 20 marbles, a 1 out of 10 chance.
why.C: Red is 6 of 20 marbles, a 3 out of 10 chance.
why.D: Yellow is 8 of 20 marbles, a 2 out of 5 chance, not 1 out of 5.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: placing a number in a Venn diagram
items.prompt: The Venn diagram sorts some numbers. In which part of the diagram does the number 18 belong?
items.explanation: 18 is even (18 = 2 × 9) and a multiple of 3 (18 = 3 × 6). A number that fits both labels goes where the circles overlap.
items.misconceptions: checks only one label

why.B: Eighteen is even and a multiple of 3, so it belongs inside both circles, not outside them.
why.C: Eighteen is also 3 × 6, a multiple of 3, so it goes in the overlap.
why.D: Eighteen is also even, so it goes in the overlap.

items.subject: QR
items.subskill: reflecting a point across a line on a grid
items.prompt: The triangle on the grid is flipped over the dashed line. Where does the corner at (2, 6) land?
items.explanation: The dashed line is at 5. The corner at (2, 6) is 3 units left of it, so it lands 3 units right: 5 + 3 = 8. A flip over an upright line does not change the up number. The image is (8, 6).
items.misconceptions: miscounts the distance to the line; flips the wrong corner

why.A: (6, 2) swaps the numbers of the corner's position; a flip over an upright line keeps the up number, 6.
why.B: (7, 6) lands 2 past the line; the corner is 3 units left of the line, so it lands 3 units right of it.
why.C: (8, 2) is where the corner at (2, 2) lands; the question asks about (2, 6).
